extra.message: User-controlled request body is deserialized with pickle.loads(), allowing arbitrary code execution. The raw bytes come from either the HTTP request body or a query parameter 'blob' (line 74), which an authenticated attacker can craft to execute any Python object graph.

User input from request.GET 'expr' is passed directly into Python eval(). Although __builtins__ is stripped, the expression still has access to module-level attributes and can escape the sandbox via object introspection (e.g., using str.__class__.__bases__[0].__subclasses__() to access arbitrary classes).

User input from request.GET 'url' is passed directly to urllib.request.urlopen() without any validation or allowlist. An attacker can craft URLs pointing to internal network services (e.g., http://localhost:6379, file:///etc/passwd) to perform SSRF attacks against the server's network.

User input from request.GET 'packet_ref' is concatenated directly into a file path (BASE_EXPORT_DIR / packet_ref) without sanitization. An attacker can use '../' sequences in the parameter to traverse above BASE_EXPORT_DIR and read arbitrary files on the filesystem, such as /etc/passwd or source code.

XML parser is configured with load_dtd=True, resolve_entities=True, and no_network=False. User-controlled request.body is parsed without restriction. This allows XXE attacks where an attacker defines external entities in the XML to read local files, perform SSRF, or cause denial of service (Billion Laugh attack).

User-controlled JSON payload from request.body is passed directly to MongoDB find_one() as a query filter. An attacker can inject NoSQL operators (e.g., $gt, $ne, $regex) in the 'filter' field to bypass authentication, exfiltrate data, or perform other NoSQL injection attacks.

User input from request.GET 'fragment' is concatenated directly into a Jinja2 template string. Since the template uses Template() (not Environment with sandbox), there is no sandboxing. An attacker can craft templates that execute arbitrary Python expressions, including subprocess calls, to achieve remote code execution.

SSL certificate verification is explicitly disabled via ssl._create_unverified_context(). Combined with urllib.request.urlopen(), this makes the server vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks. An attacker on the network path can intercept or modify the response from https://partner.invalid/status.

The Origin header from the request is reflected directly into both a JSON response body and the Access-Control-Allow-Origin header with Allow-Credentials set to 'true'. This allows any origin to make authenticated cross-origin requests. The reflected origin in the JSON body also creates an XSS vector.

cwe: CWE-601: Open redirect via DOM-based path

extra.message: The response explicitly sets Content-Security-Policy to an empty string (disabling all CSP rules) and X-XSS-Protection to '0'. This removes browser-side XSS protection mechanisms that would normally be present as defense-in-depth.

The HTTP authorization bearer token from the request header is logged via logger.warning(). This exposes authentication credentials in server logs, which can be accessed by anyone with log file access or forwarded to external logging services.

cwe: CWE-532: Information Exposure through Log Files

extra.message: The endpoint returns Django's DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE environment variable and the full BASE_EXPORT_DIR filesystem path in JSON. This leaks sensitive internal configuration information that could assist attackers in crafting further attacks.

The FileResponse uses document.original_filename (a user-controlled field stored in the model) as the filename parameter for Content-Disposition header. An attacker who can upload a document with a malicious original_filename containing CRLF characters could inject additional HTTP headers.

DEBUG is set to True by default (env_bool default parameter). When DEBUG=True, Django exposes detailed error pages with stack traces, SQL queries, and settings to any user. This should never be enabled in production.

A hardcoded default SECRET_KEY fallback is used when DJANGO_SECRET_KEY environment variable is not set. Anyone deploying without setting this env var gets a predictable/known secret key, compromising session tokens, CSRF protection, and password reset tokens.

eval() is used with user-supplied expression from request.GET['expr']. Even with __builtins__ suppressed, Python expressions can access builtins through object chains: e.g., (lambda c=type(''),('').class__.__bases__[0].__subclasses__():(c.__subclasses__()) )[()] can enumerate all loaded classes and find os.popen or similar to escalate. Combined with the internal_token gate (line 19-21), any leaked token gives RCE access.
